summary: A periodic summary of the RFCs numbered in the 1900s, intended as a convenient catalogue of that block of documents. It is an informational index rather than a technical specification.

eli5.summary: It is like the table of contents for a shelf of one hundred booklets. It helps you find which booklet you want.

questions: what rfcs are in the 1900 range
subtitle: A guide to 100 RFCs covering network protocols, services, and technologies.

tldr.problem: Finding and understanding the 100 RFCs published between 1900 and 1999 is difficult without a guide.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a annotated list summarizing each RFC in the 1900-1999 range, with titles, authors, dates, and brief descriptions to help readers understand what each document covers.
tldr.outcome: Engineers and researchers can quickly survey what was standardized in this 99-RFC span, from IPv6 and DNS extensions to PPP compression protocols and web technologies.

today: RFC 1999 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful historical snapshot of Internet standards and experimental work from the mid-1990s, helping readers understand the evolution of protocols like IPv6, PPP, DNS, routing, and web standards.

sections.title: What This Summary Is
sections.content:
RFC 1999 is an index of 100 RFCs, numbered 1900 through 1999, published between February and January 1997. It lists each RFC by number, author, date, title and provides a one or two sentence description of what it covers. The purpose is to help the Internet community navigate this block of technical documents.

This is an informational document, not a technical standard. It does not specify how the network should work, but rather explains what the network community standardized during a particular period.
sections.eli5: This RFC is a list of 100 other RFCs, with a short note about what each one is about. It is like a table of contents that helps you find which RFC you need.

sections.title: The 1900s Decade of Standards
sections.content:
The RFCs covered span many areas of the Internet. The 1900-1999 range includes standards for core protocols (IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, Neighbor Discovery for IPv6), data transmission (PPP compression and encryption protocols), routing (BGP extensions and reflections), DNS extensions (NOTIFY, incremental zone transfer), security (Kerberos GSS-API, SOCKS authentication), web standards (HTTP/1.0, HTML tables, client-side image maps), network management (SNMPv2), mail protocols (POP3), and many others.

Some RFCs are Standards Track (destined to become Internet standards), while others are Experimental, Informational, or Best Current Practices. The document notes that the standards status may change, so readers should check the current "Internet Official Protocol Standards" document for the latest state.
sections.eli5: The 100 RFCs cover many different parts of the Internet: how computers talk to each other, how they handle data, how information finds the right place, and how people keep their data secure.

sections.title: Major Areas Covered
sections.content:
Routing and addressing: The 1900s saw work on BGP (the Border Gateway Protocol) and IPv6, including community attributes, route reflection, autonomous system confederations, address autoconfiguration, and neighbor discovery. Several RFCs address IPv4 address allocation and renumbering.

Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP): Numerous RFCs cover extensions to PPP for compression (deflate, BSD compress, Stac LZS, Predictor, Magnalink), encryption (DES), multilink connections, and use on different link types like Frame Relay and Ethernet.

DNS: Extensions include the NOTIFY opcode (for zone change notification) and IXFR (incremental zone transfer), which let DNS secondary servers stay synchronized more efficiently.

Web and applications: HTTP/1.0, HTML tables, client-side image maps, and LDAP (directory service) representation as URLs and search filters.

Security and authentication: Kerberos GSS-API, SOCKS Version 5, cryptographic considerations, and sequence number attack defenses.
sections.eli5: The RFCs in the 1900s cover sending data reliably between computers, finding information by name, keeping information secure, and letting people browse the web.

sections.title: How to Navigate This Index
sections.content:
Each entry in the RFC 1999 list includes the RFC number, the author, publication date, title, and a brief explanation. Entries marked [STANDARDS-TRACK] indicate RFCs on the Internet standards track, which are the most significant for interoperability.

RFC 1999 is static—it was published once in January 1997 to document the state of the 1900s. To understand the current status of any RFC listed here, consult the latest "Internet Official Protocol Standards" (STD 1), which is published regularly and tracks which RFCs have been obsoleted, updated, or promoted to full standards.
sections.eli5: To use this list, find a topic you are interested in, look up the RFC number, and then read that full RFC. The [STANDARDS-TRACK] mark shows which ones are the most important for building working networks.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 1999 is an Informational RFC that remains useful for historical context. The RFCs it summarizes have evolved: some have been obsoleted by newer standards (for example, IPv4-only protocols), some have become full Internet Standards, and some remain experimental or informational. The individual RFCs in the 1900s continue to be referenced today as foundational work on IPv6, DNS, PPP, routing, and web protocols.
sections.eli5: This summary is still useful today if you want to understand what the Internet community decided to standardize in 1996 and early 1997.

references.text: Postel, J., "Internet Official Protocol Standards", RFC 1920, March 1996.
